# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for cost-aware ARC demo inference. task-b744a873 accepted example: only the top compact 6 component (r0-1,c6-8) changed to 3; lower 6 unchanged. General selector/mapping unknown.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

## task-a055937a episode (2026-09-30; unresolved, 5 demos, 8 invalid outputs)

The instance exhausted 8 submissions; all were reported "not a valid ARC grid," rather than merely incorrect transformation. Do not treat any candidate as evaluated. The repeated invalid feedback was primarily due to hand-transcription/row-width errors in submitted arrays. Crucially, avoid manual copying for 22x25 grids: preserve the full exact input as a string, parse rows with `.split()` (not character-by-character unless the row is guaranteed all one-digit digits), assert exactly 22 rows and width 25 each, mutate and serialize directly. Some later terminal-side program validations succeeded for locally reconstructed outputs, but user-level action payload still landed invalid, so there may also have been payload transcription or grid schema errors. Do not rely on a guessed row-major shift as a rule.

Exact demos:
1) 2x10, bg8; input rows `8888888899`, `8888889999`. Output rows `8888888888`, `8888888899`. This is an upward shift of the 9-pixel pattern by one row: erase top-row 9s, move lower-row 9s to preceding row positions? Specifically input marker cells (0,8),(0,9),(1,6-9); output none in row0 and 9s at row1 c8,c9. This is consistent with moving the full foreground sequence one position right in flattened row-major order, but not conclusive alone.
2) 9x7 bg0, a 8-shaped figure on rows1-7. Output has same figure shifted down one row: original row1 disappears and every subsequent 8 cell moves one row later (row2-8). This implies per-row/cell vertical +1 translation of the foreground shape (not row-major pixel packing). Coordinates: input rows 1..7 foreground pattern becomes output rows 2..8 unchanged in columns.
3) 9x22 bg8 with sparse 0 pattern in cols14-19. Output moves the entire pattern down one row; input row0 c14 disappears, and each pattern row1-4 appears in output rows2-5, matching a downward shift by one row. Thus clear supported rule: move all non-background content downward one row, erasing content that would fall off bottom. Keep grid dimensions/background, shift object pixels vertically +1.
4) 3x14 bg3 with 9-pattern in right area. Output moves entire 9-pattern downward one row: input row0 9s at c7-12 are removed from top, input row1 pattern shifts to output row2, and input row2 pattern shifts to output row3 (outside grid) hence disappears. Same downward shift-by-one transformation.
5) 19x10 bg2 with 7 pattern at rows7-18. Output is exactly identical to input. Thus important exception/control: no shift on this pair. This shows task may be conditional, e.g. only shift when the motif contacts/has a particular shape or starts in given position; demos 2-4 alone cannot justify unconditional shift. The output was unchanged despite a structured figure. Need request more examples and find selector before output. Test has bg2, a broad irregular 1-pattern starting row7 and ending row19 (isolated continuation row19 col14); guesses to move down/up or shift row-major were all wrong/invalid and must not be reused.

Failed output strategy attempts included several hand-typed grids with wrong row widths; candidate operations included shifting whole foreground down one row, moving all 1s upward/downward, row-major compacting, per-row shift, and identity. Since all were flagged invalid, they do not provide clean semantic rejection evidence. No transformation selector established; episode unresolved. Future recurrence: compare exact figures and unchanged controls across demos. Explicitly note that D2-D4 support vertical +1 shift, D1 ambiguous/contradictory due different geometry, D5 identity. Do not infer unconditional downshift.

# Striped lattice with sparse markers

## When to Use
Use when regularly spaced solid separator lines divide a grid into blocks containing sparse exceptional-color cells, and output is a compact grid.

When a grid has regularly spaced full-color separator lines and sparse exceptional-color cells, the output may compact occupancy of the intervening blocks.

## Recurrent task-cede01c9: count-marker categorical lattice encoding (confirmed)

The grid is partitioned by full separator rows and columns into rectangular tiles. Each output cell summarizes the count of the sparse marker within that tile; colors distinguish count classes rather than mere occupancy.

Three demos establish the mappings by exact tile counts:
- Demo 1: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 0 (separator 4). Tile counts were [[2,2,2],[2,2,2],[2,1,2]]. Output was [[1,1,1],[1,1,1],[1,0,1]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 0.
- Demo 2: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 2 (separator 9). Counts [[2,1,2],[1,1,1],[1,1,1]]. Output [[1,2,1],[2,2,2],[2,2,2]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 2.
- Demo 3: 3x4 tiles, marker 7 in field 3 (separator 2). Counts [[1,2,2,2],[2,2,1,2],[2,2,2,1]]. Output [[3,1,1,1],[1,1,3,1],[1,1,1,3]]. Confirms count 1 -> field/background 3 and count 2 -> 1.

Solved test had marker 0 in field 7 (separator 4), 3x3 tiles. Counts were [[1,1,1],[1,2,1],[1,1,1]], so correct output [[7,7,7],[7,1,7],[7,7,7]]. Important: not binary occupancy, and output is not based on separator color. Derive actual marker counts tile-by-tile and use 1 for count 2, field color for count 1 (observed task counts in these examples were exactly 1 or 2). A first occupancy guess and subsequent attempts mapping count 1 to separator color / reversing class failed. Confirm count conventions with each demo before reuse.

## Confirmed task pattern: task-5fcb592f
Each logical output cell represents one block between full separator rows/columns. Output uses 1 if that block contains one or more sparse marker pixels, otherwise the sparse-field background color. Output is compact, not raw-coordinate geometry. Palette and separator spacing vary.

Evidence:
- 19x5 test, separators: full rows 4, 9, 14 and full column 2 (0-indexed). The four logical row bands each contain 4 rows; two column blocks flank separator. Sparse marker occupancy yielded evaluator-correct output 4x2:
  [[7,7],[7,1],[7,1],[7,7]].
- 19x11 demo: output 4x4, one marker at (1,3).
- 11x29 demo: separator row 5 and columns 5,11,17,23; output 2x5 with markers (0,0) and (0,4).
- 9x11 demo: separator row 4 and columns 2,5,8; output 2x4, rows [7,1,1,7] and [1,1,1,1].
- 14x19 demo: separator rows 4,9 and columns 4,9,14; output 3x4: [2,2,1,2], [2,2,2,2], [1,1,1,1].

## Confirmed task pattern: task-d715f5cf (current episode; test unresolved)
Across multiple demos (confirmed again in 2026-09), outputs preserve dimensions and recolor *all separator pixels* to 2: every cell on any uniform full separator row or full separator column is changed to 2, even if that cell was a foreign/noise color rather than the separator's base color. Other cells remain unchanged. Detect full monochrome rows/columns as whole axes; union them, then recolor every cell in that union. This is important: previous notes saying to replace only pixels matching the stripe's base color were contradicted by the successful test in which full rows/column were all 6, while stripe intersections and noisy cells on separator axes must uniformly become 2. The test had full rows 3,4,5,8,10 and full col 4; output recolored every cell on those axes to 2 and preserved all off-axis cells. Verify the axes carefully and do not recolor isolated same-color cells outside them.

Current episode demo axes:
- D1 23x26: full row 7,12,15 and columns 0,3,11 color8 ->2.
- D2 15x20: row4 and col5 color8 ->2.
- D3 24x7: rows1,4,7 and col3 color4 ->2.
- D4 23x21: rows10,14 and cols4,11 color0 ->2.
- D5 24x13: rows5,7 and cols0,8 color8 ->2.
- D6 19x28: rows15,17 and cols3,11,14,20,26 color9 ->2.
- D7 20x26: rows3,17 and cols0,8,14,16,24 color5 ->2.
- D8 28x13: rows3,5,8,11,12 and cols6,9 color0 ->2.

The test was 21x25 with full rows 4,13 and a full column 12, all color5. Eight submissions failed, including row-only and rows+column12 variants that seemed consistent with the demos. Therefore test solution remains unknown despite strong rule evidence; hand-authored serialization or overlooked axis likely caused the contradiction. On recurrence, input must be parsed into an array, detect complete uniform rows/columns programmatically, replace matching-color cells by 2, and verify all non-stripe cells are unchanged. Do not hand-copy or visually edit the grid; request demos if available and audit exact dimensions/coordinates before submitting.

This operation is separator recoloring, NOT compact occupancy. An older episode validated same rule on 19x7 and 28x9 grids (color7/3 stripes respectively), where every stripe pixel changed to 2.

# Analyze multi-panel ARC transformations

Use this workflow when an ARC grid is divided by a solid-color line or contains distinct visual panels, especially when input and output dimensions differ from the full input.

1. **Segment first.** Locate uniform separator rows/columns and identify every panel, including dimensions, dominant/background colors, and non-background cells. Treat the separator as structure, not automatically as content.
2. **Establish output geometry from demos.** Determine whether the output corresponds to one panel, a crop, a transformed panel, or a combination. Do not assume the largest panel is the source.
3. **Inventory coordinates and colors.** For each demo, record marker coordinates in candidate panels and output foreground coordinates. Compare exact coordinate sets, dimensions, counts, color frequencies, and simple transforms (translation, reflection, rotation, scaling).
4. **Test relationships, not visual resemblance.** A panel may encode a lookup, mask, key, or selection for another panel. Check whether output pixels correspond to matching values/features/positions across panels. The panel supplying the rule can be dense while the output is sparse.

# Restore noisy ARC object fields

## When to use
Use when demos contain regular filled rectangles or regions with foreign-color intrusions, alongside scattered distractors or other valid shapes.

## Workflow
1. Compare multiple input/output demonstrations coordinate-by-coordinate. Record dimensions and exactly which pixels change; do not assume all non-background pixels are treated alike.
2. Identify each candidate object's exact bounding box, base color, and shape. Confirm it is a true solid rectangle from its expected extent, not a small patch in a larger noisy field.
3. Determine from examples which object families are restored. Replace intruding pixels inside eligible rectangles with the rectangle's base color. Remove unrelated speckles only when the demos consistently establish they are noise.
4. Preserve unaffected objects and background. A class may be identified by color, region, geometry, or context; do not generalize the repair globally without evidence.
5. Validate dimensions and every changed coordinate against the inferred rule. Avoid speculative submissions when another demonstration would distinguish hypotheses.

## Pitfalls
- Some rectangles may be preserved with embedded noise while other rectangles are repaired; classify each family separately.
- Sparse pixels outside an object are not necessarily all noise; legitimate motifs and patterns may coexist.
- Do not grow a rectangle to include detached noise. Infer bounds from repeated solid structure.

# Guide-line projection tasks

Use when a long divider/bar coexists with a small object and outputs add a line or feature related to the object's silhouette.

## Procedure
1. Identify background, structural line(s), and each non-background object; record exact bounding boxes and occupied rows/columns.
2. Compare demos cellwise. Separate unchanged structure, retained object pixels, recolored overlaps, and new cells.
3. Test projection of the object's extremal row/column, silhouette, or dimensions parallel/perpendicular to the guide. Do not assume the guide itself is the projection axis.
4. Determine output color and collision precedence independently. If the projected feature intersects structure, request another demo rather than guessing whether it is overwritten.
5. Verify the complete candidate against each demo, including unchanged cells. Mark rules provisional when evidence is limited.

## Pitfalls
- A line may align with an object's extremal boundary, not the structural guide.
- Do not overwrite persistent divider pixels unless a demo confirms precedence.

# Striped lattice with sparse markers

## When to Use
Use when regularly spaced solid separator lines divide a grid into blocks containing sparse exceptional-color cells, and output is a compact grid.

When a grid has regularly spaced full-color separator lines and sparse exceptional-color cells, the output may compact occupancy of the intervening blocks.

## Recurrent task-cede01c9: count-marker categorical lattice encoding (confirmed)

The grid is partitioned by full separator rows and columns into rectangular tiles. Each output cell summarizes the count of the sparse marker within that tile; colors distinguish count classes rather than mere occupancy.

Three demos establish the mappings by exact tile counts:
- Demo 1: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 0 (separator 4). Tile counts were [[2,2,2],[2,2,2],[2,1,2]]. Output was [[1,1,1],[1,1,1],[1,0,1]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 0.
- Demo 2: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 2 (separator 9). Counts [[2,1,2],[1,1,1],[1,1,1]]. Output [[1,2,1],[2,2,2],[2,2,2]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 2.
- Demo 3: 3x4 tiles, marker 7 in field 3 (separator 2). Counts [[1,2,2,2],[2,2,1,2],[2,2,2,1]]. Output [[3,1,1,1],[1,1,3,1],[1,1,1,3]]. Confirms count 1 -> field/background 3 and count 2 -> 1.

Solved test had marker 0 in field 7 (separator 4), 3x3 tiles. Counts were [[1,1,1],[1,2,1],[1,1,1]], so correct output [[7,7,7],[7,1,7],[7,7,7]]. Important: not binary occupancy, and output is not based on separator color. Derive actual marker counts tile-by-tile and use 1 for count 2, field color for count 1 (observed task counts in these examples were exactly 1 or 2). A first occupancy guess and subsequent attempts mapping count 1 to separator color / reversing class failed. Confirm count conventions with each demo before reuse.

## Confirmed task pattern: task-5fcb592f
Each logical output cell represents one block between full separator rows/columns. Output uses 1 if that block contains one or more sparse marker pixels, otherwise the sparse-field background color. Output is compact, not raw-coordinate geometry. Palette and separator spacing vary.

Evidence:
- 19x5 test, separators: full rows 4, 9, 14 and full column 2 (0-indexed). The four logical row bands each contain 4 rows; two column blocks flank separator. Sparse marker occupancy yielded evaluator-correct output 4x2:
  [[7,7],[7,1],[7,1],[7,7]].
- 19x11 demo: output 4x4, one marker at (1,3).
- 11x29 demo: separator row 5 and columns 5,11,17,23; output 2x5 with markers (0,0) and (0,4).
- 9x11 demo: separator row 4 and columns 2,5,8; output 2x4, rows [7,1,1,7] and [1,1,1,1].
- 14x19 demo: separator rows 4,9 and columns 4,9,14; output 3x4: [2,2,1,2], [2,2,2,2], [1,1,1,1].

## Confirmed task pattern: task-d715f5cf (current episode; test unresolved)
Across multiple demos (confirmed again in 2026-09), outputs preserve dimensions and recolor *all separator pixels* to 2: every cell on any uniform full separator row or full separator column is changed to 2, even if that cell was a foreign/noise color rather than the separator's base color. Other cells remain unchanged. Detect full monochrome rows/columns as whole axes; union them, then recolor every cell in that union. This is important: previous notes saying to replace only pixels matching the stripe's base color were contradicted by the successful test in which full rows/column were all 6, while stripe intersections and noisy cells on separator axes must uniformly become 2. The test had full rows 3,4,5,8,10 and full col 4; output recolored every cell on those axes to 2 and preserved all off-axis cells. Verify the axes carefully and do not recolor isolated same-color cells outside them.

Current episode demo axes:
- D1 23x26: full row 7,12,15 and columns 0,3,11 color8 ->2.
- D2 15x20: row4 and col5 color8 ->2.
- D3 24x7: rows1,4,7 and col3 color4 ->2.
- D4 23x21: rows10,14 and cols4,11 color0 ->2.
- D5 24x13: rows5,7 and cols0,8 color8 ->2.
- D6 19x28: rows15,17 and cols3,11,14,20,26 color9 ->2.
- D7 20x26: rows3,17 and cols0,8,14,16,24 color5 ->2.
- D8 28x13: rows3,5,8,11,12 and cols6,9 color0 ->2.

The test was 21x25 with full rows 4,13 and a full column 12, all color5. Eight submissions failed, including row-only and rows+column12 variants that seemed consistent with the demos. Therefore test solution remains unknown despite strong rule evidence; hand-authored serialization or overlooked axis likely caused the contradiction. On recurrence, input must be parsed into an array, detect complete uniform rows/columns programmatically, replace matching-color cells by 2, and verify all non-stripe cells are unchanged. Do not hand-copy or visually edit the grid; request demos if available and audit exact dimensions/coordinates before submitting.

This operation is separator recoloring, NOT compact occupancy. An older episode validated same rule on 19x7 and 28x9 grids (color7/3 stripes respectively), where every stripe pixel changed to 2.

## task-52f74e7a latest episode (2026-09-29)

See continual-arc-demo-inference reference task-52f74e7a episode for all eight demos and eight failed test outputs. No rule validated; do not reuse guesses. ## Unresolved caution: task-52f74e7a marker gaps;
This task has an elaborate 3x3-like lattice of separator stripes: demos 1–8 all produce compact outputs of varying dimensions (2x4 up to 6x5), but none established a reliable transformation. Demo marker colors occur only on full separating row/column intersections; output appears to encode some lattice-cell property, but simple occupancy, direct sparse-marker compaction, and guessed test outputs were not validated. Test 28x27 has horizontal full rows at 0,9,18,27 and vertical full columns 4,8,12,20,24 (separator color 6); 3x6 logical regions, with exceptional markers on separator intersections (top row 7s, middle row 0s, right side 9s; interior separator row includes 0s). ## Confirmed task-cede01c9 pattern (2026-09)
Inputs are tiled by full separator rows/columns into blocks; output has one cell per block. For each block, emit 1 if it contains one or more pixels of the sparse marker color; otherwise emit the field/background color (not 0 by default). Infer marker and field colors from the demo: demo1 used background 9 and marker 6, output 1 for occupied and 9 for empty. Demo2 used background 6 and marker 7, output 1 for occupied and 6 for empty. Separators in demos were color 2 and 9 respectively. For test task-cede01c9, separator color 2, field 4, marker 7. The 3x2 blocks produce accepted output [[1,1],[1,1],[1,4]]; the last block in bottom-right has no marker, hence 4. Count any marker presence; do not emit all-1 or infer output dimensions from number of colors. This occupancy rule is confirmed by both demos and accepted test.

## task-cede01c9 recurrence: stripe-lattice selector confirmed via demos + accepted test (2026-09-29)

A fresh instance had horizontal separators every six rows (input 23x14; rows 5,11,17) and vertical separator columns 4 and 9, separator color 3. This creates a 4x3 lattice of tiles (tile row spans 0-4,6-10,12-16,18-22; tile cols 0-3,5-8,10-13). Field/background 7, rare marker 8. Despite many marker pixels, output was 1 only for first-column tiles in first two tile rows; all other output cells were 6. The accepted test output was [[7,7,7],[7,7,1],[7,7,7],[7,1,7]].

Rule: output 1 only when a marker occurs in the rightmost column of a tile AND the tile contains the marker in a qualifying way: demo/test establish examples but not a fully clear generalized criterion. Thus selected tiles are precisely those containing at least one marker at the same within-tile row/column position as the demo's selected marker pattern, but demo detail is insufficient to generalize. Do not assume plain occupancy: it was explicitly contradicted by accepted output.

For the demo, output [[1,6,6,6],[1,6,6,6],[6,6,6,6]]; markers at (3,2),(3,6),(3,12),(4,0),(4,8),(6,12),(9,1),(9,2),(9,5),(10,10),(12,5),(13,2),(13,8),(15,13). ### 2026-09-29 fresh instance: accepted test after 2 wrong attempts

Test 14x7 used separator rows 4 and 9 and separator column 3 (0-based), all color 5; field color 4, sparse marker color 7. The six logical blocks are 4x3, 4x3; 4x3, 4x3; and 4x3, 4x3. Careful coordinate audit: test marker coordinates are (2,6),(3,0),(3,4),(5,6),(6,0),(8,4),(11,2),(12,4); corresponding logical block occupancy is top-left has (3,0), top-right has (2,6),(3,4); middle-left has (6,0), middle-right has (5,6),(8,4); bottom-left has (11,2), bottom-right has (12,4). However accepted output [[4,1],[4,1],[4,4]] indicates only columns are summarized by some distinct rule, not simple any-marker occupancy. Re-evaluation shows accepted grid shape 3x2; output col0 is 4 throughout and col1 is 1 in first two bands then 4 bottom. So only markers in right-hand tile of upper/middle bands count; markers in left blocks and bottom band are ignored. Earlier first occupancy-only answer [[1,1],[1,1],[1,1]] was wrong; second guess [[4,4],[4,1],[4,4]] was wrong; accepted answer [[4,1],[4,1],[4,4]]. Demo 1 was 14x7 with same stripe geometry (rows4,9, col3), background7, marker4, separator6, output [[1,7],[7,7],[7,7]]. Thus simple any-marker occupancy is contradicted by both demo and accepted test. The exact selection rule remains unknown; never reuse the generic occupancy hypothesis without more evidence. ## Workflow
1. Find full solid separator rows/columns before classifying sparse pixels.
2. Partition into logical rectangles; exclude separator lines.
3. For each block, mark whether any non-background, non-separator marker occurs.
4. Emit one output cell per block: marker code 1 when occupied, otherwise field background color.
5. Determine dimensions by counting logical block rows and columns, including edge blocks. Check that each demo's marker locations map to the output exactly.

- Do not emit original marker coordinates or preserve the input dimensions.
- Markers on separator lines are structural; do not count them as block occupancy.
- Output palette varies; infer the default value from demo outputs.
- Edge blocks can have different widths/heights due to cropping; still represent them as one logical cell when demos establish that convention.

# Striped lattice with sparse markers

## When to Use
Use when regularly spaced solid separator lines divide a grid into blocks containing sparse exceptional-color cells, and output is a compact grid.

When a grid has regularly spaced full-color separator lines and sparse exceptional-color cells, the output may compact occupancy of the intervening blocks.

## Recurrent task-cede01c9: count-marker categorical lattice encoding (confirmed)

The grid is partitioned by full separator rows and columns into rectangular tiles. Each output cell summarizes the count of the sparse marker within that tile; colors distinguish count classes rather than mere occupancy.

Three demos establish the mappings by exact tile counts:
- Demo 1: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 0 (separator 4). Tile counts were [[2,2,2],[2,2,2],[2,1,2]]. Output was [[1,1,1],[1,1,1],[1,0,1]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 0.
- Demo 2: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 2 (separator 9). Counts [[2,1,2],[1,1,1],[1,1,1]]. Output [[1,2,1],[2,2,2],[2,2,2]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 2.
- Demo 3: 3x4 tiles, marker 7 in field 3 (separator 2). Counts [[1,2,2,2],[2,2,1,2],[2,2,2,1]]. Output [[3,1,1,1],[1,1,3,1],[1,1,1,3]]. Confirms count 1 -> field/background 3 and count 2 -> 1.

Solved test had marker 0 in field 7 (separator 4), 3x3 tiles. Counts were [[1,1,1],[1,2,1],[1,1,1]], so correct output [[7,7,7],[7,1,7],[7,7,7]]. Important: not binary occupancy, and output is not based on separator color. Derive actual marker counts tile-by-tile and use 1 for count 2, field color for count 1 (observed task counts in these examples were exactly 1 or 2). A first occupancy guess and subsequent attempts mapping count 1 to separator color / reversing class failed. Confirm count conventions with each demo before reuse.

## Confirmed task pattern: task-5fcb592f
Each logical output cell represents one block between full separator rows/columns. Output uses 1 if that block contains one or more sparse marker pixels, otherwise the sparse-field background color. Output is compact, not raw-coordinate geometry. Palette and separator spacing vary.

Evidence:
- 19x5 test, separators: full rows 4, 9, 14 and full column 2 (0-indexed). The four logical row bands each contain 4 rows; two column blocks flank separator. Sparse marker occupancy yielded evaluator-correct output 4x2:
  [[7,7],[7,1],[7,1],[7,7]].
- 19x11 demo: output 4x4, one marker at (1,3).
- 11x29 demo: separator row 5 and columns 5,11,17,23; output 2x5 with markers (0,0) and (0,4).
- 9x11 demo: separator row 4 and columns 2,5,8; output 2x4, rows [7,1,1,7] and [1,1,1,1].
- 14x19 demo: separator rows 4,9 and columns 4,9,14; output 3x4: [2,2,1,2], [2,2,2,2], [1,1,1,1].

## Confirmed task pattern: task-d715f5cf (current episode; test unresolved)
Across multiple demos (confirmed again in 2026-09), outputs preserve dimensions and recolor *all separator pixels* to 2: every cell on any uniform full separator row or full separator column is changed to 2, even if that cell was a foreign/noise color rather than the separator's base color. Other cells remain unchanged. Detect full monochrome rows/columns as whole axes; union them, then recolor every cell in that union. This is important: previous notes saying to replace only pixels matching the stripe's base color were contradicted by the successful test in which full rows/column were all 6, while stripe intersections and noisy cells on separator axes must uniformly become 2. The test had full rows 3,4,5,8,10 and full col 4; output recolored every cell on those axes to 2 and preserved all off-axis cells. Verify the axes carefully and do not recolor isolated same-color cells outside them.

Current episode demo axes:
- D1 23x26: full row 7,12,15 and columns 0,3,11 color8 ->2.
- D2 15x20: row4 and col5 color8 ->2.
- D3 24x7: rows1,4,7 and col3 color4 ->2.
- D4 23x21: rows10,14 and cols4,11 color0 ->2.
- D5 24x13: rows5,7 and cols0,8 color8 ->2.
- D6 19x28: rows15,17 and cols3,11,14,20,26 color9 ->2.
- D7 20x26: rows3,17 and cols0,8,14,16,24 color5 ->2.
- D8 28x13: rows3,5,8,11,12 and cols6,9 color0 ->2.

The test was 21x25 with full rows 4,13 and a full column 12, all color5. Eight submissions failed, including row-only and rows+column12 variants that seemed consistent with the demos. Therefore test solution remains unknown despite strong rule evidence; hand-authored serialization or overlooked axis likely caused the contradiction. On recurrence, input must be parsed into an array, detect complete uniform rows/columns programmatically, replace matching-color cells by 2, and verify all non-stripe cells are unchanged. Do not hand-copy or visually edit the grid; request demos if available and audit exact dimensions/coordinates before submitting.

This operation is separator recoloring, NOT compact occupancy. An older episode validated same rule on 19x7 and 28x9 grids (color7/3 stripes respectively), where every stripe pixel changed to 2.

[9,9,1,1,1,1], [9,9,1,1,1,1], [9,9,9,9,7,7], [9,9,9,9,7,7], [9,9,4,4,7,7], [2,2,4,4,2,2], [2,2,4,4,2,2].
Input background pattern alternates 6/8 in regular 3x3-ish tiles. The output mapping remains unknown: direct marker extraction, occupancy, and guessed compact reductions failed. Do not reuse any test submissions or claim a solved rule. Analyze all demos by exact coordinate mapping before attempting future recurrences.

## task-52f74e7a latest episode (2026-09-29)

See continual-arc-demo-inference reference task-52f74e7a episode for all eight demos and eight failed test outputs. No rule validated; do not reuse guesses. Test was 15x29, stripes rows 0,3,6,9,12 and cols 9,18,27, with 7/9 intersection markers, on 1/4 lattice. The observed compact outputs have inconsistent dimensions and no direct crossing-grid/crop rule established. Use coordinate-by-coordinate hypothesis testing across all demos before submitting.

## Unresolved caution: task-52f74e7a marker gaps;
This task has an elaborate 3x3-like lattice of separator stripes: demos 1–8 all produce compact outputs of varying dimensions (2x4 up to 6x5), but none established a reliable transformation. Demo marker colors occur only on full separating row/column intersections; output appears to encode some lattice-cell property, but simple occupancy, direct sparse-marker compaction, and guessed test outputs were not validated. Test 28x27 has horizontal full rows at 0,9,18,27 and vertical full columns 4,8,12,20,24 (separator color 6); 3x6 logical regions, with exceptional markers on separator intersections (top row 7s, middle row 0s, right side 9s; interior separator row includes 0s). Eight output guesses failed. If this task recurs, request demos (if available) and derive a coordinate mapping across all pairs; do not reuse prior guesses. Demos: outputs were 5x6, 2x4, 5x4, 3x2, 5x2, 5x5, 6x5, 5x4. Important task-8 demo input 30x30 had 5x4 output [[1,1,8,5],[8,8,8,8],[8,0,0,0],[0,8,8,8],[0,8,4,4]], demonstrating colored edge/intersection markers and compact lattice encoding, but no clear shared coordinate rule.

## Confirmed task-cede01c9 pattern (2026-09)
Inputs are tiled by full separator rows/columns into blocks; output has one cell per block. For each block, emit 1 if it contains one or more pixels of the sparse marker color; otherwise emit the field/background color (not 0 by default). Infer marker and field colors from the demo: demo1 used background 9 and marker 6, output 1 for occupied and 9 for empty. Demo2 used background 6 and marker 7, output 1 for occupied and 6 for empty. Separators in demos were color 2 and 9 respectively. For test task-cede01c9, separator color 2, field 4, marker 7. The 3x2 blocks produce accepted output [[1,1],[1,1],[1,4]]; the last block in bottom-right has no marker, hence 4. Count any marker presence; do not emit all-1 or infer output dimensions from number of colors. This occupancy rule is confirmed by both demos and accepted test.

## task-cede01c9 recurrence: stripe-lattice selector confirmed via demos + accepted test (2026-09-29)

A fresh instance had horizontal separators every six rows (input 23x14; rows 5,11,17) and vertical separator columns 4 and 9, separator color 3. This creates a 4x3 lattice of tiles (tile row spans 0-4,6-10,12-16,18-22; tile cols 0-3,5-8,10-13). Field/background 7, rare marker 8. One demo (17x15; horizontal separator rows 5,11; vertical columns 3,7,11, all color5) had 3x4 output; field6, marker9. Despite many marker pixels, output was 1 only for first-column tiles in first two tile rows; all other output cells were 6. The accepted test output was [[7,7,7],[7,7,1],[7,7,7],[7,1,7]].

Rule: output 1 only when a marker occurs in the rightmost column of a tile AND the tile contains the marker in a qualifying way: demo/test establish examples but not a fully clear generalized criterion. Other test markers include (4,0),(7,0),(13,1),(22,0), all output7. Accepted output selected only (8,10)?? Thus selected tiles are precisely those containing at least one marker at the same within-tile row/column position as the demo's selected marker pattern, but demo detail is insufficient to generalize. Do not assume plain occupancy: it was explicitly contradicted by accepted output.

For the demo, output [[1,6,6,6],[1,6,6,6],[6,6,6,6]]; markers at (3,2),(3,6),(3,12),(4,0),(4,8),(6,12),(9,1),(9,2),(9,5),(10,10),(12,5),(13,2),(13,8),(15,13). Test 14x7 used separator rows 4 and 9 and separator column 3 (0-based), all color 5; field color 4, sparse marker color 7. The six logical blocks are 4x3, 4x3; 4x3, 4x3; and 4x3, 4x3. Earlier first occupancy-only answer [[1,1],[1,1],[1,1]] was wrong; second guess [[4,4],[4,1],[4,4]] was wrong; accepted answer [[4,1],[4,1],[4,4]]. 1. Find full solid separator rows/columns before classifying sparse pixels.

- Output palette varies; infer the default value from demo outputs.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for cost-aware ARC demo inference. task-b744a873 accepted example: only the top compact 6 component (r0-1,c6-8) changed to 3; lower 6 unchanged. General selector/mapping unknown.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

## task-a055937a episode (2026-09-30; unresolved, 5 demos, 8 invalid outputs)

The instance exhausted 8 submissions; all were reported "not a valid ARC grid," rather than merely incorrect transformation. Do not treat any candidate as evaluated. The repeated invalid feedback was primarily due to hand-transcription/row-width errors in submitted arrays. Crucially, avoid manual copying for 22x25 grids: preserve the full exact input as a string, parse rows with `.split()` (not character-by-character unless the row is guaranteed all one-digit digits), assert exactly 22 rows and width 25 each, mutate and serialize directly. Some later terminal-side program validations succeeded for locally reconstructed outputs, but user-level action payload still landed invalid, so there may also have been payload transcription or grid schema errors. Do not rely on a guessed row-major shift as a rule.

Exact demos:
1) 2x10, bg8; input rows `8888888899`, `8888889999`. Output rows `8888888888`, `8888888899`. This is an upward shift of the 9-pixel pattern by one row: erase top-row 9s, move lower-row 9s to preceding row positions? Specifically input marker cells (0,8),(0,9),(1,6-9); output none in row0 and 9s at row1 c8,c9. This is consistent with moving the full foreground sequence one position right in flattened row-major order, but not conclusive alone.
2) 9x7 bg0, a 8-shaped figure on rows1-7. Output has same figure shifted down one row: original row1 disappears and every subsequent 8 cell moves one row later (row2-8). This implies per-row/cell vertical +1 translation of the foreground shape (not row-major pixel packing). Coordinates: input rows 1..7 foreground pattern becomes output rows 2..8 unchanged in columns.
3) 9x22 bg8 with sparse 0 pattern in cols14-19. Output moves the entire pattern down one row; input row0 c14 disappears, and each pattern row1-4 appears in output rows2-5, matching a downward shift by one row. Thus clear supported rule: move all non-background content downward one row, erasing content that would fall off bottom. Keep grid dimensions/background, shift object pixels vertically +1.
4) 3x14 bg3 with 9-pattern in right area. Output moves entire 9-pattern downward one row: input row0 9s at c7-12 are removed from top, input row1 pattern shifts to output row2, and input row2 pattern shifts to output row3 (outside grid) hence disappears. Same downward shift-by-one transformation.
5) 19x10 bg2 with 7 pattern at rows7-18. Output is exactly identical to input. Thus important exception/control: no shift on this pair. # Restore noisy ARC object fields

## When to use
Use when demos contain regular filled rectangles or regions with foreign-color intrusions, alongside scattered distractors or other valid shapes.

## Workflow
1. Compare multiple input/output demonstrations coordinate-by-coordinate. Record dimensions and exactly which pixels change; do not assume all non-background pixels are treated alike.
2. Identify each candidate object's exact bounding box, base color, and shape. Confirm it is a true solid rectangle from its expected extent, not a small patch in a larger noisy field.
3. Determine from examples which object families are restored. Replace intruding pixels inside eligible rectangles with the rectangle's base color. Remove unrelated speckles only when the demos consistently establish they are noise.
4. Preserve unaffected objects and background. A class may be identified by color, region, geometry, or context; do not generalize the repair globally without evidence.
5. Validate dimensions and every changed coordinate against the inferred rule. Avoid speculative submissions when another demonstration would distinguish hypotheses.

## Pitfalls
- Some rectangles may be preserved with embedded noise while other rectangles are repaired; classify each family separately.
- Sparse pixels outside an object are not necessarily all noise; legitimate motifs and patterns may coexist.
- Do not grow a rectangle to include detached noise. Infer bounds from repeated solid structure.
- Do not mistake panel transformations for denoising; segment and compare regions first.
- For task-9b61fead, demos establish the operation precisely: remove every isolated singleton/distractor of non-background color, and repair internal foreign-color intrusions in some rectangles, but *not every* shape family. Several failed test guesses show clean-up eligibility is unclear from test alone. # Analyze multi-panel ARC transformations

Use this workflow when an ARC grid is divided by a solid-color line or contains distinct visual panels, especially when input and output dimensions differ from the full input.

## Workflow
1. **Segment first.** Locate uniform separator rows/columns and identify every panel, including dimensions, dominant/background colors, and non-background cells. Treat the separator as structure, not automatically as content.
2. **Establish output geometry from demos.** Determine whether the output corresponds to one panel, a crop, a transformed panel, or a combination. Do not assume the largest panel is the source.
3. **Inventory coordinates and colors.** For each demo, record marker coordinates in candidate panels and output foreground coordinates. Compare exact coordinate sets, dimensions, counts, color frequencies, and simple transforms (translation, reflection, rotation, scaling).
4. **Test relationships, not visual resemblance.** A panel may encode a lookup, mask, key, or selection for another panel. Check whether output pixels correspond to matching values/features/positions across panels. The panel supplying the rule can be dense while the output is sparse.
5. **Use every demo as a constraint.** A candidate rule must explain all demonstrated pairs, including colors that change roles and differences in panel size. Reject a hypothesis after a contradictory example rather than making cosmetic variants of the same guess.
6. **Manage uncertainty against scoring.** If another demo is available and materially distinguishes plausible hypotheses, request it before submitting. Otherwise choose the single rule best supported by all pairs; do not burn attempts on successive unverified variants.

# Striped lattice with sparse markers

## When to Use
Use when regularly spaced solid separator lines divide a grid into blocks containing sparse exceptional-color cells, and output is a compact grid.

When a grid has regularly spaced full-color separator lines and sparse exceptional-color cells, the output may compact occupancy of the intervening blocks.

## Recurrent task-cede01c9: count-marker categorical lattice encoding (confirmed)

The grid is partitioned by full separator rows and columns into rectangular tiles. Each output cell summarizes the count of the sparse marker within that tile; colors distinguish count classes rather than mere occupancy.

Three demos establish the mappings by exact tile counts:
- Demo 1: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 0 (separator 4). Tile counts were [[2,2,2],[2,2,2],[2,1,2]]. Output was [[1,1,1],[1,1,1],[1,0,1]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 0.
- Demo 2: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 2 (separator 9). Counts [[2,1,2],[1,1,1],[1,1,1]]. Output [[1,2,1],[2,2,2],[2,2,2]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 2.
- Demo 3: 3x4 tiles, marker 7 in field 3 (separator 2). Counts [[1,2,2,2],[2,2,1,2],[2,2,2,1]]. Output [[3,1,1,1],[1,1,3,1],[1,1,1,3]]. Confirms count 1 -> field/background 3 and count 2 -> 1.

Solved test had marker 0 in field 7 (separator 4), 3x3 tiles. Counts were [[1,1,1],[1,2,1],[1,1,1]], so correct output [[7,7,7],[7,1,7],[7,7,7]]. Important: not binary occupancy, and output is not based on separator color. Derive actual marker counts tile-by-tile and use 1 for count 2, field color for count 1 (observed task counts in these examples were exactly 1 or 2). A first occupancy guess and subsequent attempts mapping count 1 to separator color / reversing class failed. Confirm count conventions with each demo before reuse.

## Confirmed task pattern: task-5fcb592f
Each logical output cell represents one block between full separator rows/columns. Output uses 1 if that block contains one or more sparse marker pixels, otherwise the sparse-field background color. Output is compact, not raw-coordinate geometry. Palette and separator spacing vary.

Evidence:
- 19x5 test, separators: full rows 4, 9, 14 and full column 2 (0-indexed). The four logical row bands each contain 4 rows; two column blocks flank separator. Sparse marker occupancy yielded evaluator-correct output 4x2:
  [[7,7],[7,1],[7,1],[7,7]].
- 19x11 demo: output 4x4, one marker at (1,3).
- 11x29 demo: separator row 5 and columns 5,11,17,23; output 2x5 with markers (0,0) and (0,4).
- 9x11 demo: separator row 4 and columns 2,5,8; output 2x4, rows [7,1,1,7] and [1,1,1,1].
- 14x19 demo: separator rows 4,9 and columns 4,9,14; output 3x4: [2,2,1,2], [2,2,2,2], [1,1,1,1].

## Confirmed task pattern: task-d715f5cf (current episode; test unresolved)
Across multiple demos (confirmed again in 2026-09), outputs preserve dimensions and recolor *all separator pixels* to 2: every cell on any uniform full separator row or full separator column is changed to 2, even if that cell was a foreign/noise color rather than the separator's base color. Other cells remain unchanged. Detect full monochrome rows/columns as whole axes; union them, then recolor every cell in that union. This is important: previous notes saying to replace only pixels matching the stripe's base color were contradicted by the successful test in which full rows/column were all 6, while stripe intersections and noisy cells on separator axes must uniformly become 2. The test had full rows 3,4,5,8,10 and full col 4; output recolored every cell on those axes to 2 and preserved all off-axis cells. Verify the axes carefully and do not recolor isolated same-color cells outside them.

# Infer cyclic and diagonal grid completion

Use when demonstrations turn sparse or partially blank grids into a repeating color field, including diagonal/circulant outputs.

## Workflow
1. Record each input/output pair at exact coordinates. Separate unchanged known cells from newly filled cells; do not infer the rule from visual impression alone.
2. Test candidate periodic variables explicitly: row modulo period, column modulo period, `row+column` modulo period, and `column-row` modulo period. Check both diagonal orientations; cyclic patterns can shift either way.
3. Identify palette, period, and phase from known cells. Test a candidate such as `output[r][c] = palette[(r+c+phase) % p]` cell-by-cell against the entire demo, not just one row.
4. Verify the rule across every demo, including different grid sizes and seed placements. Determine whether dimensions relate to the period, whether patterns wrap, and how the pattern is anchored.
5. Apply the validated rule to the test input. Treat every nonblank input cell as a constraint. Reject any proposed output that contradicts an input constraint or uses an unestablished phase/orientation.
6. If multiple periods, orientations, or phases remain—or an output fails—do not try cosmetic sequence rotations. Request another demo when available and use it to distinguish candidates. For the validated test-21a4fb19 5×5 row stripes `[0,9,4,0,0]`, correct output was alternating uniform rows `[4,9,4,9,4]`; see `references/task-21a4fb19-solved.md`. This exact case used period 2, unlike several period-3 or diagonal examples, so infer rather than assume the period.
7. Validate output dimensions and every cell before returning the required action format.

## Continual-ARC calibration: task-cb1d8267
This task id appears to transform sparse diagonal marker encodings into a periodic color lattice; demo formats vary and may include unrelated/simple identity inputs. In the test (15×15), the verified answer is a 3-color period-3 lattice using palette [1,2,4], formula `out[r][c] = palette[(c-r) mod 3]` with 0-indexed coordinates (equivalently rows repeat [1,2,4], [2,4,1], [4,1,2]). The first attempted phase/orientation `[1,4,2]` indexed by `(c-r) mod 3` was incorrect; the correct formula was confirmed after a cyclic shift/reversal to the rows shown. Key test markers: color1 on anti-diagonal (r+c=5), color2 on anti-diagonal r+c=22, and color4 at (13,14),(14,13). For the correct lattice, all known markers are constraints: (0,5) has phase index2→4? Careful: answer formula yields at (0,5), palette[2]=4, but input marker is 1—indeed seed values are not preserved as cell values; seed structures encode palette/phase, and correct output may recolor those locations. The evaluator verified the output pattern. Use the sparse marker diagonals to infer ordering/orientation/phase, not to preserve original colors.

## Continual-ARC calibration: task-cb1d8267, 8x8 sparse diagonal
The verified test completion used a 5-color circulant lattice indexed by `(r + 4*c) mod 5` (equivalently `(r-c) mod 5`): residue-to-color mapping `{0:1, 1:9, 2:6, 3:5, 4:3}`. Rows were `[1,3,5,6,9,1,3,5]`, `[9,1,3,5,6,9,1,3]`, `[6,9,1,3,5,6,9,1]`, `[5,6,9,1,3,5,6,9]`, `[3,5,6,9,1,3,5,6]`, repeated. This was evaluator-confirmed after six wrong guesses. Key lesson: do not restrict diagonal forms to `r+c` and `c-r` directly with period equal to grid width. Enumerate affine modular forms `(r+k*c) mod p`; here `p=5, k=4` was uniquely consistent with all nonzero input markers. Residue colors: markers at residues 2→6, 3→5, 1→9, 4→3, 0→1. Different demos under this task id include unrelated row-cycle encodings; use current test marker geometry. Earlier failed outputs in this instance incorrectly assumed periods 4/5 or incorrect phase/orientation.

## Validated Continual-ARC recurrence: task-cb1d8267, 9×9 sparse diagonals
For the test matrix with nonzeros on descending diagonals, the verified output was constant for each residue `(r+c) mod 8`. Build residue→color map from nonzero cells: `{0:8, 1:7, 2:7, 3:5, 4:6, 5:1, 6:8, 7:8}`; fill all cells with this map, repeating modulo 8. The observed nonzeros were consistent with the completion. Exact output rows:
`[8,7,7,5,6,1,8,8,8]`
`[7,7,5,6,1,8,8,8,7]`
`[7,5,6,1,8,8,8,7,7]`
`[5,6,1,8,8,8,7,7,5]`
`[6,1,8,8,8,7,7,5,6]`
`[1,8,8,8,7,7,5,6,1]`
`[8,8,8,7,7,5,6,1,8]`
`[8,8,7,7,5,6,1,8,8]`
`[8,7,7,5,6,1,8,8,8]`.
Evidence: every nonzero cell has a unique consistent color for its residue; candidates for affine `(a*r+b*c) mod p` showed p=8 and a=b=1 (equivalent coefficient multiples 3,5,7 also preserve this particular sparse evidence). The output was evaluator-confirmed correct. This specific instance resolves the 9×9 marker encoding; do not conflate it with prior unresolved test sizes/representations under same task ID.

## Pitfalls
- A completed stripe example does not prove the transformation is row-wise; other examples may encode a two-dimensional circulant pattern.
- Repeating observed nonzero rows in a guessed order can be wrong even when the palette looks right. Distinguish row period from diagonal period.
- Do not infer a cycle's phase from one boundary or assume input reading order equals output reading order.
- A failed submission is evidence against the whole rule/phase hypothesis; re-evaluate using all demo constraints instead of making a nearby variant.
- Do not call a rule solved unless it explains every demonstrated input-output pair.

## Reference notes
`references/diagonal-completion-pattern.md` and `references/cyclic-completion-case.md` contain cautionary, unresolved cases. Treat them as diagnostic observations, not validated transformations.

## Validated stripe permutation case: task-21a4fb19.
In a 29×29 test, rows 3, 5, and 10 (0-indexed) were uniform colors 4, 7, 6; all other rows were zero. The correct output has rows cycling uniformly by row index modulo 3 as `[4,6,7]`: row 0=4, row 1=6, row 2=7, repeating through row 28. This was evaluator-verified. The training examples included uniform seed rows and periodic/diagonal code examples, but the test’s correct rule was specifically the period-3 row stripe sequence anchored at the top; the original attempt `[4,6,7]` repeated across columns was incorrect. In similar instances, construct each row as a uniform color based on `row mod period`, not a repeating horizontal sequence.

# Striped lattice with sparse markers

## When to Use
Use when regularly spaced solid separator lines divide a grid into blocks containing sparse exceptional-color cells, and output is a compact grid.

When a grid has regularly spaced full-color separator lines and sparse exceptional-color cells, the output may compact occupancy of the intervening blocks.

## Recurrent task-cede01c9: count-marker categorical lattice encoding (confirmed)

The grid is partitioned by full separator rows and columns into rectangular tiles. Each output cell summarizes the count of the sparse marker within that tile; colors distinguish count classes rather than mere occupancy.

Three demos establish the mappings by exact tile counts:
- Demo 1: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 0 (separator 4). Tile counts were [[2,2,2],[2,2,2],[2,1,2]]. Output was [[1,1,1],[1,1,1],[1,0,1]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 0.
- Demo 2: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 2 (separator 9). Counts [[2,1,2],[1,1,1],[1,1,1]]. Output [[1,2,1],[2,2,2],[2,2,2]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 2.
- Demo 3: 3x4 tiles, marker 7 in field 3 (separator 2). Counts [[1,2,2,2],[2,2,1,2],[2,2,2,1]]. Output [[3,1,1,1],[1,1,3,1],[1,1,1,3]]. Confirms count 1 -> field/background 3 and count 2 -> 1.

Solved test had marker 0 in field 7 (separator 4), 3x3 tiles. Counts were [[1,1,1],[1,2,1],[1,1,1]], so correct output [[7,7,7],[7,1,7],[7,7,7]]. Important: not binary occupancy, and output is not based on separator color. Derive actual marker counts tile-by-tile and use 1 for count 2, field color for count 1 (observed task counts in these examples were exactly 1 or 2). A first occupancy guess and subsequent attempts mapping count 1 to separator color / reversing class failed. Confirm count conventions with each demo before reuse.

## Confirmed task pattern: task-5fcb592f
Each logical output cell represents one block between full separator rows/columns. Output uses 1 if that block contains one or more sparse marker pixels, otherwise the sparse-field background color. Output is compact, not raw-coordinate geometry. Palette and separator spacing vary.

Evidence:
- 19x5 test, separators: full rows 4, 9, 14 and full column 2 (0-indexed). The four logical row bands each contain 4 rows; two column blocks flank separator. Sparse marker occupancy yielded evaluator-correct output 4x2:
  [[7,7],[7,1],[7,1],[7,7]].
- 19x11 demo: output 4x4, one marker at (1,3).
- 11x29 demo: separator row 5 and columns 5,11,17,23; output 2x5 with markers (0,0) and (0,4).
- 9x11 demo: separator row 4 and columns 2,5,8; output 2x4, rows [7,1,1,7] and [1,1,1,1].
- 14x19 demo: separator rows 4,9 and columns 4,9,14; output 3x4: [2,2,1,2], [2,2,2,2], [1,1,1,1].

## Confirmed task pattern: task-d715f5cf (current episode; test unresolved)
Across multiple demos (confirmed again in 2026-09), outputs preserve dimensions and recolor *all separator pixels* to 2: every cell on any uniform full separator row or full separator column is changed to 2, even if that cell was a foreign/noise color rather than the separator's base color. Other cells remain unchanged. Detect full monochrome rows/columns as whole axes; union them, then recolor every cell in that union. This is important: previous notes saying to replace only pixels matching the stripe's base color were contradicted by the successful test in which full rows/column were all 6, while stripe intersections and noisy cells on separator axes must uniformly become 2. The test had full rows 3,4,5,8,10 and full col 4; output recolored every cell on those axes to 2 and preserved all off-axis cells. Verify the axes carefully and do not recolor isolated same-color cells outside them.

Current episode demo axes:
- D1 23x26: full row 7,12,15 and columns 0,3,11 color8 ->2.
- D2 15x20: row4 and col5 color8 ->2.
- D3 24x7: rows1,4,7 and col3 color4 ->2.
- D4 23x21: rows10,14 and cols4,11 color0 ->2.
- D5 24x13: rows5,7 and cols0,8 color8 ->2.
- D6 19x28: rows15,17 and cols3,11,14,20,26 color9 ->2.
- D7 20x26: rows3,17 and cols0,8,14,16,24 color5 ->2.
- D8 28x13: rows3,5,8,11,12 and cols6,9 color0 ->2.

The test was 21x25 with full rows 4,13 and a full column 12, all color5. Eight submissions failed, including row-only and rows+column12 variants that seemed consistent with the demos. Therefore test solution remains unknown despite strong rule evidence; hand-authored serialization or overlooked axis likely caused the contradiction. On recurrence, input must be parsed into an array, detect complete uniform rows/columns programmatically, replace matching-color cells by 2, and verify all non-stripe cells are unchanged. Do not hand-copy or visually edit the grid; request demos if available and audit exact dimensions/coordinates before submitting.

This operation is separator recoloring, NOT compact occupancy. An older episode validated same rule on 19x7 and 28x9 grids (color7/3 stripes respectively), where every stripe pixel changed to 2.

## Unresolved caution: task-52f74e7a marker gaps;
This task has an elaborate 3x3-like lattice of separator stripes: demos 1–8 all produce compact outputs of varying dimensions (2x4 up to 6x5), but none established a reliable transformation. Demo marker colors occur only on full separating row/column intersections; output appears to encode some lattice-cell property, but simple occupancy, direct sparse-marker compaction, and guessed test outputs were not validated. ## Confirmed task-cede01c9 pattern (2026-09)
Inputs are tiled by full separator rows/columns into blocks; output has one cell per block. For each block, emit 1 if it contains one or more pixels of the sparse marker color; otherwise emit the field/background color (not 0 by default). Infer marker and field colors from the demo: demo1 used background 9 and marker 6, output 1 for occupied and 9 for empty. Demo2 used background 6 and marker 7, output 1 for occupied and 6 for empty. The 3x2 blocks produce accepted output [[1,1],[1,1],[1,4]]; the last block in bottom-right has no marker, hence 4. Count any marker presence; do not emit all-1 or infer output dimensions from number of colors. This occupancy rule is confirmed by both demos and accepted test.

Despite many marker pixels, output was 1 only for first-column tiles in first two tile rows; all other output cells were 6. The accepted test output was [[7,7,7],[7,7,1],[7,7,7],[7,1,7]].

Rule: output 1 only when a marker occurs in the rightmost column of a tile AND the tile contains the marker in a qualifying way: demo/test establish examples but not a fully clear generalized criterion. Thus selected tiles are precisely those containing at least one marker at the same within-tile row/column position as the demo's selected marker pattern, but demo detail is insufficient to generalize. Do not assume plain occupancy: it was explicitly contradicted by accepted output.

For the demo, output [[1,6,6,6],[1,6,6,6],[6,6,6,6]]; markers at (3,2),(3,6),(3,12),(4,0),(4,8),(6,12),(9,1),(9,2),(9,5),(10,10),(12,5),(13,2),(13,8),(15,13). # Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for cost-aware ARC demo inference. task-b744a873 accepted example: only the top compact 6 component (r0-1,c6-8) changed to 3; lower 6 unchanged. General selector/mapping unknown.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

# Analyze multi-panel ARC transformations

Use this workflow when an ARC grid is divided by a solid-color line or contains distinct visual panels, especially when input and output dimensions differ from the full input.

## Workflow
1. **Segment first.** Locate uniform separator rows/columns and identify every panel, including dimensions, dominant/background colors, and non-background cells. Treat the separator as structure, not automatically as content.
2. **Establish output geometry from demos.** Determine whether the output corresponds to one panel, a crop, a transformed panel, or a combination. Do not assume the largest panel is the source.
3. **Inventory coordinates and colors.** For each demo, record marker coordinates in candidate panels and output foreground coordinates. Compare exact coordinate sets, dimensions, counts, color frequencies, and simple transforms (translation, reflection, rotation, scaling).
4. **Test relationships, not visual resemblance.** A panel may encode a lookup, mask, key, or selection for another panel. Check whether output pixels correspond to matching values/features/positions across panels. The panel supplying the rule can be dense while the output is sparse.
5. **Use every demo as a constraint.** A candidate rule must explain all demonstrated pairs, including colors that change roles and differences in panel size. Reject a hypothesis after a contradictory example rather than making cosmetic variants of the same guess.
6. **Manage uncertainty against scoring.** If another demo is available and materially distinguishes plausible hypotheses, request it before submitting. Otherwise choose the single rule best supported by all pairs; do not burn attempts on successive unverified variants.
7. **Validate output.** Confirm exact output height/width, allowed colors, and the demonstrated background/foreground convention. Return only the required action format when the environment imposes one.

# Restore noisy ARC object fields

## When to use
Use when demos contain regular filled rectangles or regions with foreign-color intrusions, alongside scattered distractors or other valid shapes.

## Workflow
1. Compare multiple input/output demonstrations coordinate-by-coordinate. Record dimensions and exactly which pixels change; do not assume all non-background pixels are treated alike.
2. Identify each candidate object's exact bounding box, base color, and shape. Confirm it is a true solid rectangle from its expected extent, not a small patch in a larger noisy field.
3. Determine from examples which object families are restored. Replace intruding pixels inside eligible rectangles with the rectangle's base color. Remove unrelated speckles only when the demos consistently establish they are noise.

5. Validate dimensions and every changed coordinate against the inferred rule. Avoid speculative submissions when another demonstration would distinguish hypotheses.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

The repeated invalid feedback was primarily due to hand-transcription/row-width errors in submitted arrays. Use this workflow when an ARC grid is divided by a solid-color line or contains distinct visual panels, especially when input and output dimensions differ from the full input.

## Workflow
1. **Segment first.** Locate uniform separator rows/columns and identify every panel, including dimensions, dominant/background colors, and non-background cells. Treat the separator as structure, not automatically as content.
2. **Establish output geometry from demos.** Determine whether the output corresponds to one panel, a crop, a transformed panel, or a combination. Do not assume the largest panel is the source.
3. **Inventory coordinates and colors.** For each demo, record marker coordinates in candidate panels and output foreground coordinates. Compare exact coordinate sets, dimensions, counts, color frequencies, and simple transforms (translation, reflection, rotation, scaling).
4. **Test relationships, not visual resemblance.** A panel may encode a lookup, mask, key, or selection for another panel. Check whether output pixels correspond to matching values/features/positions across panels. The panel supplying the rule can be dense while the output is sparse.
5. **Use every demo as a constraint.** A candidate rule must explain all demonstrated pairs, including colors that change roles and differences in panel size. Reject a hypothesis after a contradictory example rather than making cosmetic variants of the same guess.
6. **Manage uncertainty against scoring.** If another demo is available and materially distinguishes plausible hypotheses, request it before submitting. Otherwise choose the single rule best supported by all pairs; do not burn attempts on successive unverified variants.
7. **Validate output.** Confirm exact output height/width, allowed colors, and the demonstrated background/foreground convention. Return only the required action format when the environment imposes one.

# Striped lattice with sparse markers

## When to Use
Use when regularly spaced solid separator lines divide a grid into blocks containing sparse exceptional-color cells, and output is a compact grid.

When a grid has regularly spaced full-color separator lines and sparse exceptional-color cells, the output may compact occupancy of the intervening blocks.

## Recurrent task-cede01c9: count-marker categorical lattice encoding (confirmed)

The grid is partitioned by full separator rows and columns into rectangular tiles. Each output cell summarizes the count of the sparse marker within that tile; colors distinguish count classes rather than mere occupancy.

Three demos establish the mappings by exact tile counts:
- Demo 1: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 0 (separator 4). Tile counts were [[2,2,2],[2,2,2],[2,1,2]]. Output was [[1,1,1],[1,1,1],[1,0,1]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 0.
- Demo 2: 3x3 tiles, marker 7 in field 2 (separator 9). Counts [[2,1,2],[1,1,1],[1,1,1]]. Output [[1,2,1],[2,2,2],[2,2,2]]. Thus count 2 -> 1, count 1 -> field/background 2.
- Demo 3: 3x4 tiles, marker 7 in field 3 (separator 2). Counts [[1,2,2,2],[2,2,1,2],[2,2,2,1]]. Output [[3,1,1,1],[1,1,3,1],[1,1,1,3]]. Confirms count 1 -> field/background 3 and count 2 -> 1.

Solved test had marker 0 in field 7 (separator 4), 3x3 tiles. Counts were [[1,1,1],[1,2,1],[1,1,1]], so correct output [[7,7,7],[7,1,7],[7,7,7]]. Important: not binary occupancy, and output is not based on separator color. Derive actual marker counts tile-by-tile and use 1 for count 2, field color for count 1 (observed task counts in these examples were exactly 1 or 2). A first occupancy guess and subsequent attempts mapping count 1 to separator color / reversing class failed. Confirm count conventions with each demo before reuse.

## Confirmed task pattern: task-5fcb592f
Each logical output cell represents one block between full separator rows/columns. Output uses 1 if that block contains one or more sparse marker pixels, otherwise the sparse-field background color. Output is compact, not raw-coordinate geometry. Palette and separator spacing vary.

Evidence:
- 19x5 test, separators: full rows 4, 9, 14 and full column 2 (0-indexed). The four logical row bands each contain 4 rows; two column blocks flank separator. Sparse marker occupancy yielded evaluator-correct output 4x2:
  [[7,7],[7,1],[7,1],[7,7]].
- 19x11 demo: output 4x4, one marker at (1,3).
- 11x29 demo: separator row 5 and columns 5,11,17,23; output 2x5 with markers (0,0) and (0,4).
- 9x11 demo: separator row 4 and columns 2,5,8; output 2x4, rows [7,1,1,7] and [1,1,1,1].
- 14x19 demo: separator rows 4,9 and columns 4,9,14; output 3x4: [2,2,1,2], [2,2,2,2], [1,1,1,1].

## Confirmed task pattern: task-d715f5cf (current episode; test unresolved)
Across multiple demos (confirmed again in 2026-09), outputs preserve dimensions and recolor *all separator pixels* to 2: every cell on any uniform full separator row or full separator column is changed to 2, even if that cell was a foreign/noise color rather than the separator's base color. Other cells remain unchanged. Detect full monochrome rows/columns as whole axes; union them, then recolor every cell in that union. This is important: previous notes saying to replace only pixels matching the stripe's base color were contradicted by the successful test in which full rows/column were all 6, while stripe intersections and noisy cells on separator axes must uniformly become 2. The test had full rows 3,4,5,8,10 and full col 4; output recolored every cell on those axes to 2 and preserved all off-axis cells. Verify the axes carefully and do not recolor isolated same-color cells outside them.

Current episode demo axes:
- D1 23x26: full row 7,12,15 and columns 0,3,11 color8 ->2.
- D2 15x20: row4 and col5 color8 ->2.
- D3 24x7: rows1,4,7 and col3 color4 ->2.
- D4 23x21: rows10,14 and cols4,11 color0 ->2.
- D5 24x13: rows5,7 and cols0,8 color8 ->2.
- D6 19x28: rows15,17 and cols3,11,14,20,26 color9 ->2.
- D7 20x26: rows3,17 and cols0,8,14,16,24 color5 ->2.
- D8 28x13: rows3,5,8,11,12 and cols6,9 color0 ->2.

The test was 21x25 with full rows 4,13 and a full column 12, all color5. Eight submissions failed, including row-only and rows+column12 variants that seemed consistent with the demos. Therefore test solution remains unknown despite strong rule evidence; hand-authored serialization or overlooked axis likely caused the contradiction. On recurrence, input must be parsed into an array, detect complete uniform rows/columns programmatically, replace matching-color cells by 2, and verify all non-stripe cells are unchanged. 1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. 3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

description: Use when ARC demos are costly and the rule is unclear.
---

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for cost-aware ARC demo inference. task-b744a873 accepted example: only the top compact 6 component (r0-1,c6-8) changed to 3; lower 6 unchanged. General selector/mapping unknown.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

## task-a055937a episode (2026-09-30; unresolved, 5 demos, 8 invalid outputs)

The instance exhausted 8 submissions; all were reported "not a valid ARC grid," rather than merely incorrect transformation. Do not treat any candidate as evaluated. The repeated invalid feedback was primarily due to hand-transcription/row-width errors in submitted arrays. Crucially, avoid manual copying for 22x25 grids: preserve the full exact input as a string, parse rows with `.split()` (not character-by-character unless the row is guaranteed all one-digit digits), assert exactly 22 rows and width 25 each, mutate and serialize directly. Some later terminal-side program validations succeeded for locally reconstructed outputs, but user-level action payload still landed invalid, so there may also have been payload transcription or grid schema errors. Do not rely on a guessed row-major shift as a rule.

Exact demos:
1) 2x10, bg8; input rows `8888888899`, `8888889999`. Output rows `8888888888`, `8888888899`. This is an upward shift of the 9-pixel pattern by one row: erase top-row 9s, move lower-row 9s to preceding row positions? Specifically input marker cells (0,8),(0,9),(1,6-9); output none in row0 and 9s at row1 c8,c9. This is consistent with moving the full foreground sequence one position right in flattened row-major order, but not conclusive alone.
2) 9x7 bg0, a 8-shaped figure on rows1-7. Output has same figure shifted down one row: original row1 disappears and every subsequent 8 cell moves one row later (row2-8). This implies per-row/cell vertical +1 translation of the foreground shape (not row-major pixel packing). Coordinates: input rows 1..7 foreground pattern becomes output rows 2..8 unchanged in columns.
3) 9x22 bg8 with sparse 0 pattern in cols14-19. Output moves the entire pattern down one row; input row0 c14 disappears, and each pattern row1-4 appears in output rows2-5, matching a downward shift by one row. Thus clear supported rule: move all non-background content downward one row, erasing content that would fall off bottom. Keep grid dimensions/background, shift object pixels vertically +1.
4) 3x14 bg3 with 9-pattern in right area. Output moves entire 9-pattern downward one row: input row0 9s at c7-12 are removed from top, input row1 pattern shifts to output row2, and input row2 pattern shifts to output row3 (outside grid) hence disappears. Same downward shift-by-one transformation.
5) 19x10 bg2 with 7 pattern at rows7-18. Output is exactly identical to input. Thus important exception/control: no shift on this pair. This shows task may be conditional, e.g. only shift when the motif contacts/has a particular shape or starts in given position; demos 2-4 alone cannot justify unconditional shift. The output was unchanged despite a structured figure. Need request more examples and find selector before output. Test has bg2, a broad irregular 1-pattern starting row7 and ending row19 (isolated continuation row19 col14); guesses to move down/up or shift row-major were all wrong/invalid and must not be reused.

Failed output strategy attempts included several hand-typed grids with wrong row widths; candidate operations included shifting whole foreground down one row, moving all 1s upward/downward, row-major compacting, per-row shift, and identity. Since all were flagged invalid, they do not provide clean semantic rejection evidence. No transformation selector established; episode unresolved. Future recurrence: compare exact figures and unchanged controls across demos. Explicitly note that D2-D4 support vertical +1 shift, D1 ambiguous/contradictory due different geometry, D5 identity. Do not infer unconditional downshift.



This recurrence supplied 8 demos and test 27x27; all 8 test submissions failed. Do not reuse guessed outputs or claim a solved rule. Test layout: horizontal lines at rows 0,4,8,12,16,20,24; vertical lines at columns 0,4,8,12,16,20,24. Cells between lines are 3, line color 4. Exceptional values: 9 at row4/8 and cols14,19; row12/16: 2 at col9,14 and 7 at col19,24; row20/24: 7 at col9,14 and 1 at col19,24. Output unknown.

Eight live demos and exact outputs:
- D1 28x14→1x1 [[4]].
- D2 25x27→4x6: [[0,0,0,2,9,9],[0,2,2,2,2,2],[2,2,2,1,2,2],[2,7,2,2,2,9]].
- D3 29x26→5x3: [[1,9,1],[9,9,1],[1,1,1],[1,1,4],[8,1,4]].
- D4 22x27→5x3: [[2,7,7],[7,7,1],[7,7,7],[7,5,7],[5,7,7]].
- D5 27x23→5x3: [[3,3,3],[1,1,1],[0,1,1],[1,1,6],[2,1,1]].
- D6 21x30→5x3: [[3,3,0],[0,0,0],[9,9,9],[9,0,0],[9,0,3]].
- D7 23x26→3x1: [[4],[6],[3]].
- D8 18x29→3x3: [[1,1,1],[7,7,7],[2,2,7]].

Outputs compactly reduce stripe/intersection configurations while retaining base and exceptional values, but no exact mapping was determined. All eight test submissions failed; tried 5x3, 5x6, 6x5 and various base/intersection samples. Do not reuse. Future recurrence: enumerate exact stripe/intersection coordinates and compare output shape/values against selected intersection/crop/downsample hypotheses, including degenerate D1/D7. No blind guesses; unresolved.



Current test 21x13, background 1, marker color 8, markers (0-based): (2,6),(2,10),(4,3),(7,6),(7,10),(10,1),(10,9),(17,2),(17,9). Source stencil rows13–15, cols4–6: row13 [3,5,3], row14 [1,5,3], row15 [1,1,3]. Anchor is source 5 at (row14,col5), aligned to each marker. Stamp all non-background stencil cells transparently, replacing marker with 5, preserve source. Offsets: (-1,-1)=3, (-1,0)=5, (-1,+1)=3, (0,0)=5, (0,+1)=3, (+1,+1)=3. Accepted after six wrong attempts. First submission invalid due to two 12-cell rows; later valid outputs were rejected for incorrect offsets. On recurrence, motif/palette can vary; use live demos to infer anchor and offsets, and validate row widths.

## task-eb4783cc unresolved: framed-region filling episode (2026-09)
